1.q: צַדִּ֤יק אַתָּה֙ יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֥י אָרִ֖יב אֵלֶ֑י⁠ךָ
1.note: This is the beginning of what Jeremiah said to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Jeremiah.

Here Jeremiah is speaking as if his complaint against Yahweh were **claims** that he would argue before a judge in a court of law. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yet I would still question you about what is right]

Jeremiah is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the lifestyle of the wicked]

Jeremiah is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are wicked]

Jeremiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [why do all the treacherous people thrive]

2.note: Here Jeremiah is speaking of the way that Yahweh allows wicked people to prosper as if Yahweh had **planted** them like trees that took root and **produced fruit**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have allowed them to prosper; they have also become secure. They grow strong; they have also become successful]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **you** before the information about being **Near** and **far away**. Alternate translation: [You are near in their mouth but far away from their kidneys]
Here, **their mouth** represents what they say. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in what they say]

Here Jeremiah is speaking of the innermost thoughts and affections of these people as if they were their **kidneys**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but far away from their inner thoughts]

3.note: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you test my inner thoughts toward you]

3.q: הַתִּקֵ⁠ם֙ כְּ⁠צֹ֣אן לְ⁠טִבְחָ֔ה וְ⁠הַקְדִּשֵׁ֖⁠ם לְ⁠י֥וֹם הֲרֵגָֽה
3.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please drag them away like sheep for slaughter and please set them apart for the day of slaughter]

The point of this comparison is that just as **sheep** are helpless when they are dragged away to be butchered, so are the wicked people whom Jeremiah wants Yahweh to punish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as helplessly as sheep being taken to be butchered]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **slaughter**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for the day when you will kill them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:19.

4.q: עַד־מָתַי֙ תֶּאֱבַ֣ל הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠עֵ֥שֶׂב כָּל־הַ⁠שָּׂדֶ֖ה יִיבָ֑שׁ מֵ⁠רָעַ֣ת יֹֽשְׁבֵי־בָ֗⁠הּ
4.note: Jeremiah is using the question form to lament how long the land has been suffering. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For so long the land has dried up and the herbage of every field has withered from the wickedness of those who dwell in it!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because those who dwell in it act wickedly]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people who dwell in the land, while the pronoun **He** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [because those who dwell in the land said, “Yahweh will not see our end.”]

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “He will not see our end.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “God will not see our ways.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

5.q: כִּ֣י אֶת־רַגְלִ֥ים ׀ רַ֨צְתָּה֙ וַ⁠יַּלְא֔וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵ֥יךְ תְּתַֽחֲרֶ֖ה אֶת־הַ⁠סּוּסִ֑ים
5.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said in reply to Jeremiah. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

5.q: כִּ֣י אֶת־רַגְלִ֥ים ׀ רַ֨צְתָּה֙ וַ⁠יַּלְא֔וּ⁠ךָ וְ⁠אֵ֥יךְ תְּתַֽחֲרֶ֖ה אֶת־הַ⁠סּוּסִ֑ים
5.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the troubles that Jeremiah has already endured and the greater troubles that are coming as if they were a race, first against **footmen** and then against **horses**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If lesser troubles have already exhausted you, how will you endure much greater troubles]

Yahweh is using the question form to show Jeremiah that he will not be able to endure greater troubles. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [then you will certainly not be able to compete with the horses!]
The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing Jeremiah directly, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

5.q: וּ⁠בְ⁠אֶ֤רֶץ שָׁלוֹם֙ אַתָּ֣ה בוֹטֵ֔חַ וְ⁠אֵ֥יךְ תַּעֲשֶׂ֖ה בִּ⁠גְא֥וֹן הַ⁠יַּרְדֵּֽן
5.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that Jeremiah feels secure only in **a land of peace**. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [And suppose that you feel secure only in a land of peace; in that case, how will you do in the height of the Jordan]

Yahweh is using the question form to show Jeremiah that he will not be able to cope with even greater dangers. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [then you certainly will not be able to manage in the height of the Jordan!]

Yahweh is using **the height of the Jordan** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the dense thickets that grow along the Jordan River.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the dense thickets along the Jordan River]

6.note: Here, **house** means all the people who belong to one family. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **your father’s house** figuratively means the rest of Jeremiah’s own relatives. Alternate translation: [and the rest of your father’s relatives]

Yahweh is using **they have called after you fully** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have shouted loudly against you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even they have shouted loudly against you]

6.q: מָלֵ֑א אַל־תַּאֲמֵ֣ן בָּ֔⁠ם כִּֽי־יְדַבְּר֥וּ אֵלֶ֖י⁠ךָ טוֹבֽוֹת
6.note: Yahweh uses the word **though** here to indicate a contrast between the good things that Jeremiah’s relatives say to him and the treacherous way that they actually treat him. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They speak good things to you, but do not trust in them]

7.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I have utterly abandoned my own inheritance]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a **house**, that is, a household of people who belonged to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my own people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were an **inheritance**, property that he had received and owned. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who are my own possession]

Yahweh is using **my soul** to represent himself as a whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one whom I love]

The pronoun **her** refers to the people of Judah, whom Yahweh has just called his **inheritance**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [into the hand of my people’s enemies]

Here, **hand** represents the power and control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the power of her enemies]

8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion in the forest** roars fiercely at anyone who comes near it, so Yahweh’s people speak defiantly against him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [My inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest that roars fiercely at anyone who approaches it]

Yahweh is using **uttered against me with her voice** as a common expression of the culture to mean “spoke against me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [she spoke against me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:6.

9.q: הַ⁠עַ֨יִט צָב֤וּעַ נַחֲלָתִ⁠י֙ לִ֔⁠י הַ⁠עַ֖יִט סָבִ֣יב עָלֶ֑י⁠הָ
9.note: Yahweh is using the question form to state that his people are attacking him, and they are being attacked from every side. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [My inheritance is a speckled bird of prey to me. Birds of prey are all around against her!]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were **a speckled bird of prey**, a bird whose unusual markings cause other birds to attack it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an easy target for her enemies]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the armies that will attack his people as if they were **the beast of the field** that he was calling together to eat. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [assemble all the enemy armies; bring them to devour her]

10.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the rulers who have attacked his land as if they were **shepherds** who were caring for a flock. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Many leaders]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a **vineyard** that he had planted and tended. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my people, whom I cared for like a a vinedresser would care for a vineyard]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **wilderness** that is characterized by **desolation**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a desolate wilderness]

11.note: The pronoun **He** could refer to: (1) each of the many shepherds mentioned in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [Each of those shepherds has made it a desolation] or (2) the enemy who has invaded the land. Alternate translation: [The invading enemy has made it a desolation]

Yahweh is speaking of the land as if it were a living thing that **mourns** over what has happened to it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [it lies ruined before me]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **desolate** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [it is utterly desolate]

The expression **it is made desolate** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [these enemies have made it desolate]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [because no one lays it to heart]

Yahweh is speaking of laying something **to heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “thinking seriously about something.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [no man thinks seriously about it]

12.q: עַֽל־כָּל־שְׁפָיִ֣ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֗ר בָּ֚אוּ שֹֽׁדְדִ֔ים כִּ֣י חֶ֤רֶב לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ אֹֽכְלָ֔ה מִ⁠קְצֵה־אֶ֖רֶץ וְ⁠עַד־קְצֵ֣ה הָ⁠אָ֑רֶץ אֵ֥ין שָׁל֖וֹם לְ⁠כָל־בָּשָֽׂר
12.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the sword of Yahweh is consuming from one end of the land and to the other end of the land, the destroyers have come upon all the bare heights in the wilderness; there is no peace for any flesh]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the destroyers** before the information about where they have come, **Upon all the bare heights in the wilderness**. Alternate translation: [The destroyers have come upon all the bare heights in the wilderness]

Yahweh is speaking of his **sword** as if it were a living thing that could eat and devour people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is using his sword to kill people]

Yahweh is referring to all of the land by naming two extremes, the one **end of the land** and the other. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the entire land]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [nothing is peaceful for any flesh]

Yahweh is using **flesh**, one part of a person, to represent people as a whole. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for anyone]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:13.

13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the useless results of his people’s efforts as if they had **sown wheat** and then **harvested thorns**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They have farmed hard but gained nothing useful]

Even though Yahweh has been speaking about his people in the third person as **They**, here he addresses them directly in the second person as **your**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue to speak about them in the third person here. Alternate translation: [Let them be ashamed of their harvests]
See how you translated the similar expression in 4:8.
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:11.

14.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:5.

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the first person as **my** within a sentence that speaks of him in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the third person. Alternate translation: [all his evil neighbors who strike the inheritance that he has caused his people Israel to inherit]

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that a person of this culture would commonly use to mean that he was about to do something. He is not telling the listeners to look at him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to pluck them up from upon their land]

Here Yahweh is speaking of removing these nations from their land as if he were **plucking** up plants by their roots. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [am removing them from their land]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Judah** figuratively means all the people descended from Jacob’s son Judah. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Judah]

15.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה אַֽחֲרֵי֙ נָתְשִׁ֣⁠י אוֹתָ֔⁠ם אָשׁ֖וּב וְ⁠רִֽחַמְתִּ֑י⁠ם וַ⁠הֲשִׁבֹתִ֛י⁠ם אִ֥ישׁ לְ⁠נַחֲלָת֖⁠וֹ וְ⁠אִ֥ישׁ לְ⁠אַרְצֽ⁠וֹ
15.note: This event will not happen right after Yahweh plucks up these nations. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [And it will happen that a long time after I pluck them up, I will turn and have compassion on them and bring them back, a man to his inheritance and a man to his land]

The phrase **turn and have compassion** expresses a single idea. The word **turn** tells more about **have compassion**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [I will once more have compassion on them]

Yahweh is using **a man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each person to his inheritance and each person to his land]

16.q: אִם־לָמֹ֣ד יִלְמְדוּ֩ אֶת־דַּֽרְכֵ֨י עַמִּ֜⁠י לְ⁠הִשָּׁבֵ֤עַ בִּ⁠שְׁמִ⁠י֙ חַי־יְהוָ֔ה כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר לִמְּדוּ֙ אֶת־עַמִּ֔⁠י לְ⁠הִשָּׁבֵ֖עַ בַּ⁠בָּ֑עַל וְ⁠נִבְנ֖וּ בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ עַמִּֽ⁠י
16.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that these nations will learn the ways of his people and swear by his name. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [if they truly learn the ways of my people, so that they swear by my name ‘As Yahweh lives,’ just as they have taught my people to swear by Baal, then I will build them up in the midst of my people]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **learn** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [if they truly learn]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [to swear by my name that Yahweh lives]
See how you translated this phrase in 5:2.

The expression **they will be built** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [then I will build them up in the midst of my people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of making these nations secure and prosperous among his people as if they were a house that he **built**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then they will become accepted and prosperous in the midst of my people]

17.note: Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **pluck up** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [then I will completely uproot that nation and destroy it]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8.
See how you translated “listen” in 3:13. Alternate translation: [they do not pay attention] or [they do not obey]
